html:
The Reformation is usually dated from 31 October 1517, when Martin Luther, a monk and professor at Wittenberg in Saxony, sent out his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences. The movement that followed split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches.

Indulgences were Church grants that cut the punishment due for sins, and a preacher was selling them nearby to raise money for rebuilding St Peter's in Rome. Luther's theses were meant for academic debate, but printers spread them across Germany within weeks. Without the press that began with the Gutenberg Bible, Luther might have been one more silenced critic.

His ideas went further than indulgences:

  • People are saved by faith alone, as a gift of God's grace, not by good works.
  • Scripture alone is the authority, above popes and councils.
  • All believers are priests; clergy may marry.

The Pope excommunicated him in 1521, and at the Diet of Worms that year he refused to recant before Emperor Charles V. Saxony's prince protected him, and Luther translated the Bible into German.

Other reformers followed, Zwingli in Zurich and John Calvin in Geneva, and whole states chose sides. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome for his own reasons. Rome answered with the Council of Trent. A century of religious war followed, ending in the Holy Roman Empire with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
